one_line: A short walkthrough of Continue, an open-source VS Code extension for model-agnostic codebase chat, diff-based edits and markdown-defined PR review agents, positioned as complementary to Copilot.
summary: Better Stack presents Continue, an open-source VS Code extension, as a tool that removes friction around code, mainly code review, rather than writing code. Setup is a short extension install plus adding a model entry, either a cloud model with an API key or a local Llama 3 model served through Ollama, and models can be switched from the sidebar. The chat pulls context from the whole project (open files, git diffs), so explanations are repo-aware, and refactor suggestions show a reviewable diff that can be applied or rejected. The most distinctive feature shown is the review agent: a markdown file of rules (formatting, logic, security) that can be run against a PR, with prebuilt agents such as a security one, and output as PR comments or diffs. The speaker frames Continue as complementary to GitHub Copilot (Copilot for autocomplete, Continue for pre-merge checks). The video is thin: no benchmarks, no review-quality evidence, and the value claims are mostly asserted.

key_ideas.idea: Continue is pitched as a model-agnostic VS Code extension: cloud models with your own API key or free local models, switchable from the sidebar without lock-in.
key_ideas.detail: Setup is installing the extension, adding a model to the config (cloud with an API key, or a local model pulled through Ollama), then reloading.

key_ideas.idea: The main value claimed is in the work around the code (reviews, cross-checking, onboarding), not code generation.
key_ideas.detail: The speaker frames the bottleneck as slow code review and PR cycles, and says AI should automate the repetitive parts.

key_ideas.idea: Chat answers are repo-aware because Continue pulls context from open files and git diffs, versus pasting snippets into a browser chat.
key_ideas.detail: Highlight code, press Ctrl+L, ask 'explain this'. The speaker concedes Claude Code and Cursor can do similar things.

key_ideas.idea: Suggested edits come as a real side-by-side diff in chat that the user applies, edits or rejects.
key_ideas.detail: The speaker stresses the user keeps control, contrasted with agents that take over the editor.

key_ideas.idea: Review agents are defined as plain markdown rule files and run against a PR, instead of waiting for a human reviewer.
key_ideas.detail: Rules cover formatting, logic issues and security. Prebuilt agents exist, e.g. a security one. Output is PR comments or suggested diffs, and the same agents can run outside the editor with triggers and Slack alerts.

key_ideas.idea: Positioning: Copilot helps you type, Continue helps you ship. The two are presented as complementary, not competitors.
key_ideas.detail: Suggested combo: Copilot for autocomplete, Continue for checking that code is ready to merge. Continue is said to span PRs, CI and agents, but the video does not demonstrate CI.

techniques.name: Model-agnostic Continue setup
techniques.how: Install the Continue extension in VS Code (Extensions, search 'continue', install, reload). Open settings and edit the config file, then add a model entry: a cloud model like GPT-4 or Claude with your API key, or a local model: run `ollama pull llama3` and add it under a provider. Save and reload, then switch models from the sidebar dropdown. The exact config file name and keys are not shown in the video.
techniques.when: When you want to switch between paid cloud models and free local models per task without changing tools.

techniques.name: Repo-aware explanation of unfamiliar code
techniques.how: Highlight a block of code, press Ctrl+L, and type 'explain this' in the sidebar chat. Continue adds context from open files and git diffs, so the answer reflects the whole project.
techniques.when: Onboarding to an unfamiliar codebase, or cross-checking your understanding against the actual repo.

techniques.name: Review and apply diffs in chat
techniques.how: Ask for a change (e.g. 'refactor this function'). Continue shows a side-by-side diff preview in the chat. Edit, apply or reject it.
techniques.when: Making refactors where you want to inspect every change before it lands.

techniques.name: Markdown-defined PR review agent
techniques.how: Create a markdown file with the rules you care about (formatting, logic issues, security). Run it from the chat by invoking the agent on a PR. The transcript shows the command as 'agent my agent review and run this PR', but captions make the exact invocation syntax unclear. Prebuilt agents such as a security agent are also available. Results appear as comments or suggested diffs. Agents can be managed and given triggers, and Slack can receive PR alerts.
techniques.when: Adding a consistent first-pass review (style, logic, security) to PRs, especially for solo developers or small teams wanting consistent standards.

techniques.name: Split autocomplete and review tools
techniques.how: Keep GitHub Copilot for inline autocomplete in the editor and use Continue as a separate pre-merge check on the PR.
techniques.when: When you already use Copilot and want an additional review layer without replacing it.

numbers.claim: Claimed setup time: install and get started in under a minute (speaker's claim, not measured).
Continue is free when paired with a local Ollama model; cloud models require your own API keys (cost not quantified).
No benchmarks, latency, cost or review-quality measurements are presented; video length 4:52.

hot_takes: Copilot helps you type, Continue helps you ship: the speaker positions the tools as complementary, but the video itself makes no case that Continue's review output is better than alternatives.
The speaker says Claude Code and Cursor can do the codebase-aware explanation too, which weakens the case for Continue as a distinct tool.
Continue is said to cover PRs, CI and agents, but only the editor chat and PR review agent are shown; CI is asserted, not demonstrated.
The review-agent-as-markdown-file idea is the most reusable part, and the video gives no evidence on false-positive rates or how well it works on real PRs.

relevance.why: Continue is an editor extension for individual developers; nothing here touches the proxy, memory, inference or sandbox layers.
Defining review criteria as a versioned markdown rule file is a simple pattern that fits a harness wrapping Claude Code; the video shows no checkpointing, critique or multi-agent flow.
relevance.action: If ProsHarness gets a PR-review or critique step, keep the review criteria in a markdown rules file that is loaded at run time, rather than hard-coding prompts, so it can be edited without code changes.
